```{python}
from research_site import Study

study = Study()
LANGUAGES = ["Language X", "Language Y", "Language Z"]
STAGES = ["No related languages"] + [f"{n} related language{'s' if n > 1 else ''}" for n in range(1, 7)]
```

## Summary

- We test multi-stage fine-tuning of NLLB: fine-tuning a model on related languages first, one stage per language, then on the target language, to see whether it improves translation of low-resource languages.
- **It does not help for any of the three languages tested.** In every case, chrF3 after the final fine-tuning on the target language is below the baseline.
- chrF3 tends to fall further as more related languages are added.

## The question

Low-resource languages have little training text. Related languages may share vocabulary and grammar with the target, so training on them first could give the model a better starting point.

In this study, we investigate multi-stage fine-tuning of NLLB. We begin by fine-tuning NLLB on languages related to the target language, before finally fine-tuning on the target language itself. We ask whether this staged approach improves the target language's translations, and whether adding more related languages helps more.

One danger of multi-stage fine-tuning is catastrophic forgetting. Because we're fine-tuning NLLB multiple times, later stages of fine-tuning may "overwrite" any knowledge from earlier stages.

## How it was tested

We begin by fine-tuning NLLB up to six times on languages related to the target language. Each stage of fine-tuning starts from the fine-tuned model from the previous stage. At the very last stage, we fine-tune on the target language itself. The training data is the NT, minus Romans and Revelation, and the test set is Romans and Revelation.

We choose the related languages using alignment. Within the target language's language family, we choose the languages that align best with the target language. (There are other ways to choose these languages that may be worth investigating in the future. For example, we could choose the geographically closest languages to the target language, or we could use something like [URIEL+](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18472) to determine the closest related languages.)

## Results

```{=html}
<style>.wide-first-column col:first-child { width: 16% !important; }</style>
```

::: {.wide-first-column}
```{python}
study.table(measures=["chrF3"], groups=LANGUAGES, systems=STAGES, digits=2, intervals=False, measure_column=False, group_title="Language")
```
:::

Every staged run scores below its language's baseline. The gap tends to grow as related languages are added, though not at every step.

It is possible that using [LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) or layer freezing would help with catastrophic forgetting in multi-stage fine-tuning. This is something that may be worth investigating in the future.

## Limitations

- **Single runs, no intervals.** Differences of one to two chrF3 points could be within the noise between runs.
- **Language X's later runs.** The runs for four to six related languages build on the omitted three-language step, so they may include one fewer related language than they are labeled with.
